title: Long-window skim + experiment plan (scratchpad)
content:
Quick purpose: capture paper skims + concrete experiments to try on our long-window workload (customer X, conversational transcripts). Not polished — mostly notes and TODOs.

Top takeaways (fast skim):
1) Sparse factorized attention variant (paper A): claims near-linear memory for windows up to 1M tokens by chunking into overlapping stripes + local dense + sparse global indices. Strengths: predictable memory scaling, easy to combine with rotary-style pos encodings. Weaknesses: degraded short-range fidelity in small context windows; authors use toy conv tasks primarily.

2) KV-compression via quantized low-rank projections (paper B): instead of storing full 32-bit KV, project into small basis (k=64) per layer then store quantized coefficients (8-bit). Report ~6x memory reduction with <1% perplexity hit on LMs up to 64k tokens. Implementation note: requires extra compute when decompressing for attention queries. Good candidate for older layers where activations are less critical.

3) Adaptive prefix caching (blog post): cache prefixes at different granularities based on hit rate and token reuse heuristics. Use LRU-ish eviction prioritized by expected reuse (derived from recent session patterns). Works well with batching to reduce redundant KV work.

4) Eval paper on degradation under quantization (paper C): shows localized hallucination increase when KV lossy compression applied to very recent tokens (<512) — older tokens less harmful. Suggests layered strategy: keep recent KVs high-fidelity, compress older ones aggressively.

Immediate implications for Redwood serving runtime:
- Combine (2) + (4): implement dual-tier KV storage: "hot" buckets (lossless-ish, maybe 16-bit FP or 8-bit QK with higher basis) for last N tokens (configurable), "cold" buckets (low-rank compressed) for historic tokens.
- Integrate with batching path: when a batch references overlapping prefixes, decompress shared cold chunks once per batch, reuse across requests.
- Add heuristics in smart routing / fallback: if memory pressure high, trigger aggressive cold-tier compress and optionally reduce max_window for new requests.

Planned experiments (local cluster / dedicated GPU pool):
- Experiment A: baseline: current KV as-is, run conv-sim workload (customer X real traces, 50k sessions sample). Measure latency p50/p95, GPU mem, token cost.
- Experiment B: implement low-rank compress (k=64, 8-bit) for layers 0..6 (bottom third). Keep top layers unchanged. Run same traces. Metrics: regen perplexity on held-out segments, top-k token divergence, latency overhead (decompress compute).
- Experiment C: two-tier strategy: hot window = 1024 tokens (full precision), cold compressed as in B for older tokens. Variation: hot=512 vs 2048. Observe hallucination metrics on prompts known to require immediate context.
- Experiment D: adaptive eviction + batch-aware decompress: simulate batching with realistic inter-session reuse. Measure wasted decompress ops and effective mem savings.

Quick experiment config sketch (for ops):
- workload driver: use customer X anonymized sessions (script: tools/session-playback.py --seed 42 --max-window 64k)
- model: open-variant-1.3B (local replica) to keep runs cheap; run 10k sessions per trial, 3 seeds each
- metrics hooks: token-likelihood drift, top-1 token divergence from baseline, context-dep hallucination probe set (10 curated dialogues)
- infra: dedicated pool (G4dn-style equivalent), single replica tests then small scale parallel to test amortization of decompress costs

Notes-to-self / unknowns:
- Implementation cost: low-rank projection needs training or at least a fitted basis per layer — can we use PCA on KV activations offline? How often re-fit? monthly? per-model-version?
- Decompression latency: need to microbench CPU vs GPU decompress options. Warm path: decompress on GPU if GPU memory available; cold path: CPU async decompress and stream in.
- How does this interact with our streaming responses and function calling? When we compress older tokens, ensure we don't hold back streaming/sync. Might need partial-decompress semantics.

Open questions for the team (to discuss in sync):
- acceptable hallucination delta thresholds for customer X? (Mina to confirm)
- should compressed cold-tier be model-agnostic artifact (like a sidecar store) or embedded in runtime memory format? pros/cons for snapshot and restore times.
- fallback policy design: when memory spike, do we evict cold-tier or reduce concurrency? tradeoffs.

Action items:
- [ ] Prototype offline PCA-based basis fitter on 1M KV vectors (layer 2) — script: experiments/kv_pca_fit.py (assign to Ethan)
- [ ] Add toy decompress microbench (CPU vs CUDA) and report p50/p95 (me)
- [ ] Sync with Mina on acceptable QA thresholds and get curated probe set (Mina)
- [ ] Open RFC draft for two-tier KV store in repo: docs/rfcs/kv-two-tier.md (initial outline by end of sprint)

References / links:
- paper A (sparse factorized attention): https://arxiv.org/abs/xxxx.xxxxx
- paper B (kv low-rank compress): https://arxiv.org/abs/yyyy.yyyyy
- notes on quantization degrade: internal slack thread #quant-degrade

Random heuristics idea (brain-dump):
- Instead of fixed hot-window size, score tokens by a recency*attention-weight product (estimated from prefix statistics). Keep top-K tokens in hot-tier by expected contribution to next-token distribution. Might be heavier to compute but more precise.

End-of-scratchpad. Will turn into RFC if prototype results look promising.
